title: I Should Have Kept Going
author: Summer Mulder
summary: Mulder uses two abandoned podcasts as a case study in a decision error she now regards as her most expensive: killing a growing channel because it did not directly generate revenue. The first was a business show with a working production system - one recording day a week, three or four episodes batched, handed to a team for polish and distribution - shut down on a partner's advice to cut anything without direct revenue attached. The second, made with her husband about blended families, was closed more passively: they got busy and let it go, and years later still receive messages asking for its return. Her argument is that both decisions measured the wrong thing, because the asset being built was trust and authority, which compound slowly and cannot be manufactured with a funnel or an ad budget. The hardest observation in the piece is about restarting: coming back is not picking up where you left off but starting over, because a paused audience moves on. She lands on consistency as the mechanism that builds equity, brand, credibility and confidence over time, and on the claim that most people quit and pivot before anyone has heard them. The piece ends with her deciding to begin again in her late forties, framing a restart as courage rather than failure.
points: Mulder's central claim is that a direct-revenue test is the wrong instrument for a channel whose output is trust and authority, and that applying it killed an asset that was already compounding.

The concrete lesson about restarting is the piece's most transferable: a paused audience does not wait, so returning is a genuine restart rather than a resumption, which raises the real cost of a pause.

She names the operational system that made the first podcast sustainable - one recording day weekly, batching three to four episodes, handing off to a team - which is why the shutdown was a choice rather than a capacity failure.
Her diagnosis of why most people quit is impatience with the measurement window: they pivot fast, expect instant results, and silence themselves before an audience exists to measure.
The second podcast's ending is a different failure mode worth noting - not a decision at all, but attrition by busyness, which she treats as equally costly.
quotes: The first was all about business. Solo episodes and interviews on marketing, cash flow, team leadership, client success… the real, behind-the-scenes stuff no one teaches you when you’re just trying to keep the lights on.

I still pinch myself thinking about how quickly it grew and the caliber of people I got to talk to. And I had a system: one recording day per week, batching 3–4 episodes, then handing them off to my team to polish and publish across every channel.
That podcast helped us heal. It helped others feel less alone. And again… people listened.
It’s easy to stop, especially if you’re measuring the wrong thing. But your voice matters. Your message matters.
When you come back… it’s not a “pick up where you left off” situation. It’s starting over.
Most people quit when they don’t see instant results. They pivot too fast. They silence themselves before anyone even hears them.
